content: Children weighing more than 14 kg should receive LPV/r 100/25 mg tablets. For children weighing less than 15 kg, 5 mL of RTV 80 mg/mL oral suspension is recommended. For those weighing between 15 and less than 30 kg, RTV 50 mg (using either 25 mg or 50 mg solid formulations) is appropriate. If lower-strength RTV tablets are unavailable, 100-mg RTV tablets can be used as a booster, as limited evidence suggests they are well-tolerated and acceptable. However, this dose of RTV should only be used as a boosting agent in combination with ATV or DRV. RAL granules are approved for use from birth, but their feasibility and acceptability have not been widely studied, and concerns exist about their administration in resource-limited settings. Due to the challenges of administering granules, the Paediatric Antiretroviral Working Group recommends using 25 mg chewable tablets as dispersible tablets for infants and children older than four weeks and weighing at least 3 kg. This recommendation is based on in vitro data showing solubility and bioequivalence between tablets and granules, as well as the limited availability of alternatives for this age group. However, a feasibility and acceptability study conducted in South Africa demonstrated that administering RAL granules in rural settings is possible with adequate training and counseling. To minimize dosing errors and avoid frequent dose changes, all ARV drugs, except RAL (which requires a dose change after the first week), should be dosed based on weight at the start of treatment and maintained until four weeks of age, as weight gain is limited during the first four weeks of life. Pharmacokinetic data for preterm infants are only available for AZT, with limited data and uncertainty regarding appropriate dosing for NVP, RAL, and 3TC in preterm and low-birth-weight infants. LPV/r solution should not be given to preterm infants until they reach 42 weeks of gestational age due to the risk of adverse effects. This guidance will be updated as more evidence on solid LPV/r formulations becomes available from ongoing trials. LPV/r solution should not be used for infants younger than two weeks of age, and LPV/r pellets should not be used for infants younger than three months. Dosing recommendations for LPV/r granules in newborns are based on the current FDA approval (supporting use from two weeks of age) and the substantial uncertainty, particularly for neonates weighing 2–3 kg. If no other formulation exists, one sachet twice daily may be considered for neonates older than two weeks and weighing 2–3 kg to minimize the risk of potential toxicity from overdosing. The adapted dose of ARV drugs should continue for two weeks after rifampicin treatment ends, as the enzyme-inducing effect of rifampicin fades slowly after discontinuation. The FDA recommends administering weight-based DTG doses twice daily when taken with rifampicin, based on extrapolated drug interaction data from adults. Pharmacokinetic data in children support twice-daily DTG dosing for those weighing more than 25 kg. The Paediatric Antiretroviral Working Group emphasizes the need for further evidence collection for lower weight bands but endorses immediate uptake of twice-daily DTG dosing with rifampicin for all children at least four weeks of age and weighing at least 3 kg. The heat-stable LPV/r tablet formulation must be swallowed whole and should not be split, chewed, dissolved, or crushed. An adult 200/50 mg tablet can be used for children weighing 14–<25 kg (one tablet in the morning and one in the evening) and for children weighing 25–<35 kg (two tablets in the morning and one in the evening). LPV/r liquid requires a cold chain for transport and storage. LPV/r pellets should not be used for infants younger than three months. Dosing schedules for equivalent solid dosage forms, such as LPV/r granules, approved by the FDA for use from two weeks of age, are provided. The suggested RTV dose for super-boosting to achieve a 1:1 ratio with LPV is supported by studies exploring this approach in young children receiving LPV/r. RTV oral solution dosing is based on trial-tested regimens for super-boosting. LPV/r was administered twice daily after the first week of life according to the following dosing scheme: 40/10 mg once daily for neonates weighing 2–<4 kg and 80/20 mg once daily for infants weighing more than 4 kg. Recent years have seen the development of improved ARV formulations for children, such as dispersible, scored fixed-dose combination tablets, which have replaced traditional liquid formulations. These products have simplified HIV treatment delivery for children in low-income settings. However, the proliferation of options has led to a multiplicity of formulations across regimens and weight bands, complicating procurement and supply chain management. Generic manufacturers rely on economies of scale to maintain affordable pricing, but demand fragmentation across too many duplicative products creates instability in the reliable supply of ARV dosage forms for children. The ARV Procurement Working Group and the Global Accelerator for Paediatric Formulations Network provide formulary guidance to programs on selecting optimal ARV drugs for children, defined using robust criteria. The formulary, first developed in 2011, is routinely revised to align with current WHO guidelines and available products. The current Optimal Formulary, revised in December 2020 and released in April 2021, includes seven products delivering recommended firstand second-line regimens across all weight bands for children. Programs are encouraged to procure dosage forms included in the Optimal ARV Formulary for Children. During transition periods or special circumstances (e.g., neonatal treatment, TB co-treatment, and third-line ART), dosage forms in the ARV Limited-use Formulary are sufficient to provide appropriate dosing across weight bands for children. The urgent need for better age-appropriate formulations for infants and children living with HIV remains a priority. An additional solid fixed-dose combination formulation (ABC/3TC/LPV/r granules) is in the final stage of approval. The availability of co-formulated DRV/r in a heat-stable fixed-dose combination is critical to facilitate treatment sequencing and uptake of future secondand third-line regimens for children. Future formulations containing newer drugs, such as DTG and TAF, are essential for optimizing dosing, sequencing, and harmonization across age groups. WHO will continue to work towards simplifying prescribing, dispensing, and dosing guidance while collaborating with the pharmaceutical industry and partners to develop practical recommendations for safely scaling up ART for children.
